profile.campus: Prineville, Crook County, Oregon (Meta's original data center campus, seven buildings)
profile.address: Ochoco Highway, Prineville, Crook County, Oregon, 97554
profile.reading:
Per Meta's own official data center fact sheet, this Prineville, Oregon campus (Crook County) has seen $2B+ in investment since breaking ground in 2010, employs 350+ in operational jobs once complete, and had 1,000 skilled-trade workers on site at peak construction. Meta reports $5.3M+ in direct funding to local schools and nonprofits; campus electricity use is matched with 100% clean and renewable energy as part of Meta's net-zero operations goal, with a target to be water-positive by 2030, and a Meta-supported project is adding 977 MW of new renewable energy generation in the state.

Prineville is historically significant as Meta's (then Facebook's) original, purpose-built data center campus and the birthplace of the Open Compute Project: per Facebook's own April 7, 2011 announcement, the Prineville facility achieved a Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE) of 1.07 versus roughly 1.5 for then-conventional "best practice" data centers, a 38% reduction in energy consumption compared to Facebook's existing facilities at the time, and 24% lower infrastructure costs, achieved partly through "vanity-free" server designs that eliminated unnecessary components. Facebook open-sourced these designs and mechanical CAD files as the founding act of the Open Compute Project, with early industry partners including AMD, Dell, HP, and Intel; Facebook estimated that if one-quarter of US data center capacity adopted Open Compute specifications, the resulting energy savings could power roughly 160,000 homes annually. This registry maps seven separate buildings across the Prineville campus (numbered west to east by local mapping convention), reflecting the campus's growth in phases since the original 2010 groundbreaking.

The Prineville campus operates under Oregon's Long-Term Rural Enterprise Zone program, a state incentive dating to 1985 that Facebook first used for this site starting with construction in 2010; the resulting property-tax exemption is due to expire in 2027. Crook County and Prineville officials have said the exempted tax value on the county's data centers now totals more than $130 million a year in current assessed value across city, county, and school-district taxes combined, and that the county's data center campus (Meta's buildings together with neighboring operators) has grown to roughly 11 buildings totaling about 4.6 million square feet, employing an estimated 700 people locally, according to reporting by the Bend Source and the Bend Bulletin. Meta has said it has contributed more than $5 million directly to Crook County schools and local nonprofits since construction began, and jointly funded an underground water-storage system with Apple, whose own Prineville data center sits nearby. On the cooling side, Meta's Prineville buildings use an outside-air (free-air) cooling design suited to the high desert climate of Central Oregon: outside air is drawn through louvers into a rooftop penthouse, filtered, and humidified and cooled by a pressurized-water fogging system before being distributed to server rows through a roughly 14-foot cold-aisle plenum, with facility staff describing water use at about 30% of what a comparable chilled-water data center would consume, per Data Center Dynamics reporting on the facility.

reading.body:
Meta's Prineville campus has invested $2 billion and employed 350 operational staff at full capacity since groundbreaking in 2010, making it one of the longest-running hyperscale facilities in the United States. The campus does not publish its power capacity, preventing direct comparison to the eight other Oregon facilities with public figures totaling 156.6 megawatts. Meta reports the campus uses 100 percent renewable energy and supports a 977-megawatt renewable energy project in Oregon, but the scale of compute this campus represents remains undisclosed by the operator.

Without a published power figure, the campus cannot be ranked against other major AI infrastructure by capacity. Oregon has 133 mapped data center facilities across the state, of which only eight operators publish megawatt figures. The Prineville campus's actual position in the state's AI compute footprint is therefore unknown from public sources.

Meta's commitment to renewable matching and water-positive operations by 2030 indicates the campus is designed for extended operation under climate constraints. The absence of published capacity means readers assessing whether this campus matters to AI scaling cannot determine how much compute power it represents or how its growth trajectory compares to other large operators.
